chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub, from Umar ibn Yazid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who wanted to free his slave, whose master had imposed a tax on him every year, which the master accepted. The slave acquired wealth through his trade, in addition to what he gave his master as the tax. He said: 'If he pays his master what was imposed upon him, then whatever he earns after that obligation belongs to the slave.'
Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Has not Allah, the Exalted, imposed obligations upon His servants? When they fulfill them, He does not ask them about anything else.'
I said to him: 'Can the slave give charity from what he earned and free himself after fulfilling the obligation he used to pay to his master?' He said: 'Yes, and the reward for that is his.'

I said: 'If he frees a slave who earned wealth in addition to the tax, to whom will the patronage (walayah) of the freed person belong?' He said: 'He goes and attaches himself to whomever he wishes. If he guarantees his blood money (diyah) and his indemnity (jarirah), then he is his master and inherits him.'
I said to him: 'Did the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) not say:

I said: 'If the slave whom he freed guarantees his blood money and his indemnity, does that bind him, and will he be his master and inherit him?' He said: 'That is not permissible, and a slave does not inherit a free man.'

key_terms.جَرِيرَة: Indemnity or compensation for blood money
key_terms.سَائِبَة: A slave who buys his own freedom or is freed by his own earnings
key_terms.ضَرِيبَة: Tax or fixed tribute paid by a slave to his master

ai.seo_question: What are the financial rights of a slave who pays a fixed annual tax to his master, and who inherits him upon freedom?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) uses the analogy of divine obligations to affirm the slave's financial autonomy, arguing that just as Allah does not demand beyond the prescribed duties, a master cannot claim earnings exceeding the agreed tax. The narration further clarifies the legal distinction between a slave who buys his own freedom (mudabbad) and a siba (freed by gift), establishing that the former retains the right to choose his patron provided he guarantees the master's blood money (diya), a nuance that refines the general hadith 'al-wala' liman aqad' (patronage belongs to the manumitter).
